newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German banks start to bring business home.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German banks start to bring business home.

text.p: German banks on Wednesday said they planned to pull back key business from London, Europe's leading financial centre, in order to improve Germany's stature as a leading market in the runup to European monetary union.

Deutsche Bank and Commerzbank, the nation's two largest commercial banks, said they would soon bring back deutschemark repo-business to Frankfurt in moves that come shortly after the German central bank relaxed stringent reserve policies.

Since January 1, the Bundesbank no longer requires that banks hold reserves in non-interest bearing accounts at the central bank on a portion of their business, a rule that had been in force since 1948.

Commercial banks, complaining the Bundesbank had choked off large portions of the German financial market, claimed victory after extensive lobbying efforts to broaden the German market to include more short-term and long-term instruments.
Asked whether Deutsche Bank, a key player in the repo-market would now bring back its business to Germany, the bank's designate head Rolf Breuer told journalists "that is express company policy."

While neither Deutsche nor Commerzbank revealed the actual volume of business to be retrieved, officials said the numbers mattered less than the fact that established business practices were being changed.
Breuer said the step would go a long way towards making up ground lost to London.
"The actual number is less important than the symbolic value of the move," said Hermann Remsperger, chief economist at BHF Bank and who lobbied hard for the Bundesbank's decision.

Deutsche Bank plans to conduct all of its mark business in Frankfurt in the run-up to Europe's planned monetary union and Breuer said that the "know-how assembled" would be the best way to turn Deutsche into the "Eurobank number one".

After a panel discussion including Hesse state government officials, representatives from the state central bank and industry, Breuer it was agreed that much more work was needed to further enhance Germany's financial stature.
One key component would be to introduce pension funds in Germany which would create a highly professional group of investors which able to enlive capital markets significantly.
Breuer said it was important that tax regulations be changed so that savings would not be taxed immediately but at a later stage.
"Without this type of tax de-regulation it will be impossible to achieve a more transparent German capital market," Breuer said.

The panelists also agreed that Germany had to polish up its image to convince the world that it was not true that German finance was conducted solely in smoke-filled rooms with a only a handful of key decision makers sitting on every board.
"We need to lift the veil, make Germany more transparent and show that we do business just like everyone else does in other nations," Breuer said.

But he said France still had a head-start on Germany having had the benefit of less restriction, allowing for the development of a more sophisticated market for a much longer time. Newly-relaxed regulations however gave Germany a chance to catch up, even though this may take some time, Breuer said.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke added the group's plans, which include appointing public relations group Burson-Marsteller to launch an advertising campaign, was not an altruistic undertaking.
"We are doing this for jobs and more growth" in the region he said.
